**Sonnet 130**, *"My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun"*, is a famous satire of traditional romantic poetry. During Shakespeare’s time, poets would often compare their lovers to goddesses, claiming their eyes were like the sun, their skin like snow, and their breath like perfume. 

Shakespeare rejects these ridiculous, impossible standards. He describes his mistress exactly as she is—a normal, flawed human being. Yet, in the final couplet, he declares that his love for her is just as rare and valuable as any love built on false, exaggerated comparisons.

Below is a line-by-line reading guide, combining the original text, vocabulary notes, and a modern translation based on standard literary interpretations.

---

### Quatrain 1

**Original text:**
> My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun;
> Coral is far more red, than her lips’ red:
> If snow be white, why then her breasts are **dun**;
> If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.

::: {.column-margin}
**dun:** A dull, grayish-brown color. 
**wires:** In Elizabethan poetry, blonde hair was often compared to golden wires. Here, he subverts it with "black wires."
:::

**Modern Translation:**
My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the bright sun; 
coral is far more red than her lips are. 
If snow is pure white, then her skin is a dull grayish-brown. 
If hairs can be compared to wires, then black wires grow on her head.

---

### Quatrain 2

**Original text:**
> I have seen roses **damasked**, red and white,
> But no such roses see I in her cheeks;
> And in some perfumes is there more delight
> Than in the breath that from my mistress **reeks**.

::: {.column-margin}
**damasked:** A pattern of mixed red and white (like a Damask rose).
**reeks:** Emanates or exhales. Today this means a bad smell, but in Shakespeare's time it simply meant "breathes out" (though the contrast with perfume is intentional).
:::

**Modern Translation:**
I know what perfectly blended pink, red, and white roses look like, 
but I don’t see any rosy color in her cheeks. 
And there’s much more pleasure in expensive perfumes 
than there is in the breath that my mistress exhales.

---

### Quatrain 3

**Original text:**
> I love to hear her speak, yet well I know
> That music hath a far more pleasing sound:
> I grant I never saw a goddess **go**,
> My mistress, when she walks, **treads** on the ground:

::: {.column-margin}
**go:** To walk or move.
**treads:** Walks heavily or firmly on the earth (unlike a floating spirit).
:::

**Modern Translation:**
I love to hear her voice, although I admit 
that music is much more pleasing to the ear. 
I admit I’ve never seen a goddess walking around; 
but I know that when my mistress walks, she steps firmly on the ground like a normal human.

---

### The Couplet

**Original text:**
> And yet by heaven, I think my love as **rare**,
> As any she **belied** with false compare.

::: {.column-margin}
**rare:** Unique, precious, and valuable.
**belied:** Misrepresented or lied about through false, exaggerated comparisons.
:::

**Modern Translation:**
And yet, by heaven, I believe that my love for her is just as unique and precious 
as any woman who is lied about by poets using ridiculous, false comparisons.
